docs.title: Python Mastery Path
docs.text:
Learn Python progressively through topics, modules, mini projects, and real-world projects.

The goal of this site is not merely to learn Python syntax.

The goal is to progressively develop Python mastery through deliberate practice, repetition, and project-based learning.

docs.title: Learning Progression
docs.text:
Foundations
    ↓
Capabilities
    ↓
Composition
    ↓
Creation

This progression is reflected throughout the site:

Topic Exercises
    ↓
Module Exercises
    ↓
Mini Projects
    ↓
Real-World Projects

Each level builds upon the knowledge and skills developed in the previous level.

docs.title: 1. Topic Exercises
docs.text:
Build and strengthen your understanding of core Python concepts.

Topics include:

  • Strings
  • Lists
  • Dictionaries
  • Loops
  • Functions
  • Comprehensions
  • Exceptions

These exercises focus on developing strong foundations through progressively more challenging problems.

Goal: Learn the language.

docs.title: 2. Module Exercises
docs.text:
Master the Python Standard Library one module at a time.

Modules include:

  • pathlib
  • shutil
  • json
  • csv
  • pickle
  • datetime
  • collections
  • itertools
  • functools
  • argparse
  • subprocess
  • dataclasses
  • logging
  • sqlite3
  • re

Each module contains a progression of exercises that move from discovery to practical application.

Discovery
    ↓
Application
    ↓
Composition
    ↓
Automation

Goal: Learn the tools.

docs.title: 3. Mini Projects
docs.text:
Combine multiple Python concepts and modules into practical solutions.

Examples include:

  • Downloads Organizer
  • Markdown Analyzer
  • Log File Analyzer
  • Backup Utility
  • Repository Scanner

Mini projects bridge the gap between isolated exercises and larger applications.

Goal: Learn how to combine tools.

docs.title: 4. Real-World Projects
docs.text:
Build larger projects that resemble software you might create personally or professionally.

Examples include:

  • Static Site Generator
  • Personal Knowledge Base
  • File Synchronizer
  • Documentation Generator
  • Automation Toolkit

These projects draw upon everything learned in the previous sections.

Goal: Create useful software.

docs.title: Who Is This For?
docs.text:
This site is designed for:

  • Beginners who want a structured learning path
  • Intermediate Python developers looking to deepen their skills
  • Experienced developers who want to revisit parts of Python they do not use every day
  • Anyone interested in achieving long-term Python mastery

docs.title: Exercise Philosophy
docs.text:
Exercises in Python Mastery Path begin with realistic scenarios rather than abstract coding tasks.

The goal is not merely to learn syntax.

The goal is to understand:

  • Why a Python feature is useful
  • When a Python feature becomes useful
  • How Python helps solve practical problems

For this reason, every exercise begins with a realistic scenario.

Instead of presenting tasks such as:

Create a Path object.

an exercise might begin with:

You have a notes file on your computer and want Python
to work with that file.

The intention is to help learners think:

"I've encountered that problem before."

or:

"That sounds useful."

rather than:

"Here's another coding challenge."

Every exercise is designed to introduce a real problem and help you develop the capability needed to solve it.

Problem
    ↓
Task
    ↓
Solution

rather than:

Task
    ↓
Task
    ↓
Task

The focus of Python Mastery Path is to build practical capabilities through meaningful problems.

docs.title: Philosophy
docs.text:
Python mastery is not achieved by memorizing syntax.

Python mastery comes from:

  • Practising fundamental concepts
  • Learning the Standard Library deeply
  • Combining tools to solve problems
  • Building real software

This site exists to support that journey.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The pathlib module provides an object-oriented way to work with files and directories.

Instead of treating file paths as plain strings, pathlib represents them as Path objects with useful methods for navigating directories, reading and writing files, searching for files, and manipulating filenames.

Many developers learn Python using older modules such as os and os.path. While those modules are still widely used, pathlib often provides a more readable and Pythonic approach to filesystem operations.

Understanding pathlib is an important step toward building tools such as:

  • Repository analyzers
  • Documentation generators
  • Download organizers
  • Backup utilities
  • Static site generators
  • Personal automation scripts

Throughout these exercises, you will progress from basic path operations to practical filesystem automation.

docs.title: 1. Creating Paths
docs.text:
Learn how to create and work with Path objects.

Examples:

  • Create a Path object
  • Join paths together
  • Convert paths to strings
  • Work with relative and absolute paths

docs.title: 2. Inspecting Paths
docs.text:
Learn how to examine files and directories.

Examples:

  • Check whether a path exists
  • Determine whether a path is a file
  • Determine whether a path is a directory
  • Retrieve filename information

docs.title: 3. Reading Files
docs.text:
Learn how to access file contents.

Examples:

  • Read text files
  • Read configuration files
  • Count lines in a file
  • Process file contents

docs.title: 4. Writing Files
docs.text:
Learn how to create and modify files.

Examples:

  • Write text to a file
  • Append content
  • Generate reports
  • Create markdown files

docs.title: 5. Finding Files
docs.text:
Learn how to search for files and folders.

Examples:

  • Find all Python files
  • Find markdown files
  • Search recursively
  • Build simple file scanners

docs.title: 6. Manipulating Paths
docs.text:
Learn how to work with filenames and path components.

Examples:

  • Change file extensions
  • Extract parent directories
  • Extract file names
  • Build new paths from existing paths

docs.title: 7. Directory Operations
docs.text:
Learn how to create and manage directories.

Examples:

  • Create directories
  • Create nested directories
  • Navigate directory structures
  • Prepare project folders

docs.title: 8. Filesystem Automation
docs.text:
Combine everything learned so far.

Examples:

  • Repository analyzers
  • Downloads organizers
  • File reports
  • Folder cleanup scripts

docs.title: Mastery Levels
docs.text: Each capability contains exercises organised into four levels:

docs.title: Why Learn pathlib?
docs.text:
Many practical Python tools interact with the filesystem.

The better you understand pathlib, the easier it becomes to:

  • Build CLI tools
  • Analyze repositories
  • Generate documentation
  • Organize files
  • Create automation scripts
  • Prepare for larger real-world projects

pathlib is one of the most useful modules in the Python Standard Library and serves as a foundation for many of the mini projects and real-world projects found throughout Python Mastery Path.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Before Python can work with files and directories, it needs a way to represent their locations.

This is the purpose of pathlib.Path.

Creating paths is one of the most fundamental pathlib capabilities and serves as the foundation for everything that follows, including:

  • Inspecting paths
  • Reading files
  • Writing files
  • Finding files
  • Automating filesystem tasks

By completing these exercises, you will learn how to:

  • Create Path objects
  • Combine path components
  • Build paths dynamically
  • Create paths from user and system locations
  • Generate paths for automation tasks

docs.title: Learning Progression
docs.text:
The exercises in this section are organized into four stages:

Discover
    ↓
Apply
    ↓
Compose
    ↓
Automate

Each stage builds on the previous one, gradually moving from understanding how paths are created to using path creation as part of practical automation tasks.

docs.title: Discover
docs.text:
Learn the fundamental capability.

These exercises introduce the core ideas behind creating paths with pathlib.

Goal:

👉 Learn the capability.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You keep personal notes in a text file located at:

notes/todo.txt

Before Python can work with this file, your program needs a way to represent its location on disk.

This is one of the most common uses of pathlib.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Create a Path object representing:

notes/todo.txt

Store it in a variable named path.

Print the path to the console.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Create a Path object
  • Store it in a variable named path
  • Print the path

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

The pathlib module provides a Path class.

Stronger Hint

Import Path from pathlib.

Almost There 
Path("notes/todo.txt")

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("notes/todo.txt")

print(path)

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
This is the first and most fundamental pathlib capability.

Before Python can work with a file or directory, your program needs a way to represent its location.

Path objects provide that representation and serve as the foundation for everything else you will do with pathlib.

docs.text:
Small Hint

The location should become a Path object.

Stronger Hint

Import Path from pathlib.

Path("docs/README.md")

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are writing an automation script for your Downloads folder.

The script will eventually organize files, but first it needs a way to represent the folder itself.

The folder is:

Downloads

docs.text:
Create a Path object representing:

Downloads

Store it in a variable named downloads_path.

Print the path.

docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Store it in downloads_path
  • Print the path

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

Paths can represent folders as well as files.

Stronger Hint

Almost There

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

downloads_path = Path("Downloads")

print(downloads_path)

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Many beginners subconsciously think paths are only files.

This teaches:

Path → file OR directory

which is an important mental model.

docs.title: Solution

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
Use the capability in realistic situations.

These exercises reinforce path creation through practical filesystem scenarios.

Goal:

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are writing a script that works inside a project directory.

The project folder is:

my-project

Inside it is a documentation file:

README.md

You want to create the file path by combining the project directory and file name.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Create:

my-project/README.md

using multiple Path components.

Store the result in readme_path.

Print the path.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Create a Path object for the project directory
  • Build the final file path
  • Print the result

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

A Path object can be combined with other path parts.

Stronger Hint

Look for an operator that joins paths together.

Almost There 
project_dir / "README.md"

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

project_dir = Path("my-project")

readme_path = project_dir / "README.md"

print(readme_path)

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Introduces path composition.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:

meeting.txt

docs.text:

using the / operator.

Print the path.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Create a directory path
  • Append a filename
  • Print the final path

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

Create the folder path first.

Stronger Hint

Use / to add another path component.

Almost There

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists

docs.title: Scenario

Variables can be combined with Path objects.

The / operator works with strings.

Almost There 
docs_dir / page_name

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

docs_dir = Path("docs")

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text:
Introduces dynamic path building.

This feels much closer to real software.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building a backup utility.

Backups are stored inside:

backups

Each backup belongs to a specific year.

The year is stored in:

year = "2026"

You need to create:

backups/2026

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Build the path using multiple components.

Store the result in backup_dir.

Print the path.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Create the root backup directory
  • Add the year folder
  • Print the final path

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

Each folder can be added separately.

Stronger Hint

Use / more than once if needed.

Almost There 
Path("backups") / year

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

year = "2026"

backup_dir = Path("backups") / year

print(backup_dir)

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Shows that directories can be built dynamically just like files.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are organizing project files.

A configuration file is stored in:

projects/demo/config/settings.json

Rather than writing the entire path as a string, you decide to build it from meaningful components.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Construct:

projects/demo/config/settings.json

using multiple path segments.

Store the result in settings_path.

Print the path.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Create the path step by step
  • Use the / operator
  • Print the final result

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

Each folder can be its own path component.

Stronger Hint

Chain multiple / operations.

Almost There 
Path("projects") / "demo" / "config" / "settings.json"

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

settings_path = (
    Path("projects")
    / "demo"
    / "config"
    / "settings.json"

print(settings_path)

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Demonstrates how larger paths can remain readable and maintainable.

docs.title: Compose
docs.text:
Combine multiple techniques.

These exercises bring together path creation, variables, and dynamic path building to solve larger problems.

Goal:

👉 Combine capabilities.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building a project from inside its root directory.

Your script should work no matter where the project is located on a user's computer.

The current working directory should be used as the starting point.

A log file will live in:

logs/app.log

inside the project.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Create a path representing:

[current directory]/logs/app.log

Store the result in log_path.

Print the path.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Obtain the current working directory
  • Build the rest of the path using /
  • Print the final path

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

pathlib can provide the current directory.

Stronger Hint

Look for a method on Path related to the current working directory.

Almost There 
Path.cwd()

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

log_path = Path.cwd() / "logs" / "app.log"

print(log_path)

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Introduces one of the most useful sources of paths in real programs.

docs.title: Automate
docs.text:
Create paths at scale.

These exercises focus on generating paths automatically using loops and data structures.

Goal:

👉 Automate solutions.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building a note-taking application.

A user wants note files for several topics:

topics = [
    "python",
    "pathlib",
    "automation"
]

All notes should be stored inside:

notes/

Each note should have a .md extension.

Objective

Create and print the following paths:

notes/python.md
notes/pathlib.md
notes/automation.md

Generate them using a loop.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Use the provided list
  • Build paths dynamically
  • Print each path

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

Each topic becomes part of a filename.

Stronger Hint

Use a loop to process every topic.

Almost There 
Path("notes") / f"{topic}.md"

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

topics = [
    "python",
    "pathlib",
    "automation"
]

for topic in topics:
    note_path = Path("notes") / f"{topic}.md"
    print(note_path)

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Introduces automated path generation.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are creating a backup utility.

Backup folders should be created for multiple years:

years = [
    "2024",
    "2025",
    "2026"
]

All backups live inside:

backups/

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Create and print paths representing:

backups/2024
backups/2025
backups/2026

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Use the supplied list
  • Build directory paths dynamically
  • Print every path

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

Each year becomes a directory name.

Stronger Hint

Combine the base directory with each year.

Almost There 
Path("backups") / year

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

years = [
    "2024",
    "2025",
    "2026"
]

for year in years:
    backup_dir = Path("backups") / year
    print(backup_dir)

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Shows that path generation applies equally to files and directories.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building a documentation generator.

The project contains multiple pages:

pages = [
    "index.md",
    "installation.md",
    "configuration.md"
]

All documentation files belong inside:

docs/

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Create and print the path for every page.

Expected output:

docs/index.md
docs/installation.md
docs/configuration.md

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Loop through every page
  • Create a Path object for each page
  • Print each generated path

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

Each page is already a complete filename.

Stronger Hint

Combine a shared directory with each page.

Almost There 
Path("docs") / page

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

pages = [
    "index.md",
    "installation.md",
    "configuration.md"
]

for page in pages:
    page_path = Path("docs") / page
    print(page_path)

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Introduces the concept of a reusable base path.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building a photo organizer.

Photos should be stored inside folders named after their year.

You have:

years = ["2024", "2025"]
photos = [
    "vacation.jpg",
    "birthday.jpg"
]

For every year and every photo, generate a path.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Create and print paths such as:

photos/2024/vacation.jpg
photos/2024/birthday.jpg
photos/2025/vacation.jpg
photos/2025/birthday.jpg

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Use both provided lists
  • Generate every path combination
  • Print all generated paths

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

You may need two loops.

Stronger Hint

Build the path one component at a time.

Almost There 
Path("photos") / year / photo

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

years = ["2024", "2025"]

photos = [
    "vacation.jpg",
    "birthday.jpg"
]

for year in years:
    for photo in photos:
        photo_path = Path("photos") / year / photo
        print(photo_path)

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: Introduces multi-level automated path generation.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are building a simple project scaffolding tool.

New projects should contain:

src/
tests/
docs/

A project name is provided:

project_name = "my_app"

Your script should generate the paths that would exist inside the project.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text:
Create and print:

my_app/src
my_app/tests
my_app/docs

using the provided project name and a list of directory names.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
Your program should:

  • Build paths dynamically
  • Reuse the project name
  • Generate all required paths

docs.title: Need a Hint?
docs.text:
Small Hint

The project name becomes the root directory.

Stronger Hint

Loop through the required directories.

Almost There 
Path(project_name) / directory

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Show Solution 
from pathlib import Path

project_name = "my_app"

directories = [
    "src",
    "tests",
    "docs"
]

for directory in directories:
    project_path = Path(project_name) / directory
    print(project_path)

docs.title: Why This Exercise Exists
docs.text: This is the first exercise that feels like a genuine automation task rather than merely a learning exercise.
